speechtext: Order, please. Could the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) have a chance to make his speech? Thank you.

subtopic: NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this very important debate. I think this is a very important matter, and I wish to join the previous speakers in supporting the amendment, namely that:
"Bill C-18, An Act respecting national transportation, be not now read a second time but that the Order be discharged, the Bill withdrawn and the subject-matter thereof referred to the Standing Committee on Transport."
I support this motion without reservation, and I do so for a number of reasons.
First of all, I am not in favour of opposing measures aimed at improving the situation in the transportation industry in Canada. I agree wholeheartedly, Mr. Speaker, that we must modernize and provide a framework and regulations aimed at making the market more competitive. However, I submit, with respect, that the manner in which the Government is trying to achieve this objective is entirely unacceptable, for several reasons.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, the way this Government has been reacting in recent weeks is surprising, to say the least.
First of all, when faced with the fact that it had become impossible to negotiate a decent agreement with the United States, it willingly accepted, without further argument, whatever the United States wished to impose on us. That seems to be the way the United States and in fact this Government are approaching Canada.
Second, this Government seems to be saying that what is
good for the United States will be good for Canada. What has
produced results in the United States, will, always according to the Conservatives, have positive and beneficial effects on Canada.
I may point out to Hon. Members opposite that this is not, in my opinion, a very sound philosophy and that it is certainly not the way to deal with the administration of this country. I could name a number of reasons, but there are a few that are painfully obvious. Canada's territory is larger than the United States, but on that territory we have only twenty-five million people. There are 300 million Americans, Mr. Speaker. I think this point is particularly relevant to any regulations or legislation like the Bill before the House today. There are other facts and factors. Suppose we consider the situation in the United States, which has over thirty cities with a population of over one million. How does that compare with the situation in Canada? We have only three cities with a population of over one million, so that in Canada, transportation not only has a strategic importance in providing for the movement of goods and people, it is a matter of survival.
Regional expansion depends closely if not exclusively on transportation. Any suggestion aimed at improving this sector gets my full support, but certainly not the way our friends opposite are going about it. It stands to reason that the adoption of this Bill will soon be followed by a price war, which in turn will inevitably lead to lower rates. The free market system will prevail, which is another way of saying that major shippers will undoubtedly expect to make a handsome profit. But at the expense of what or whom? My riding lies in a semirural region where transportation is a key factor and whose economic future is closely linked with transportation issues. Smaller carriers will bear the brunt of this change, they will have to pay the higher prices which will automatically flow from the reductions which major companies will get from trucking firms.
In recent weeks I held consultations with a number of interested people who, I suggest, have every reason to be concerned about this measure, and it is interesting to note how much the views vary from one individual to the next. Still these consultations enabled me to draw two conclusions. First we have the major companies which rely on the transportation system for doing most of their business. They are unanimous: any endeavour aimed at the outright deregulation of the transport industry gets their immediate and full support. Ask them why they endorse complete deregulation and you will not have to wait for the answer: There will be drastic cuts in transportation costs, and this can only be a boost for most companies.
But go and ask the same question to small carriers and small manufacturers, and of course the answer is not quite as definite, a lot more confusing. These people are extremely worried, worried about the next day, worried about the future.
I should think there is no inconsistency in the two attitudes, the two answers, or the two reactions I have just described.
First of all, in the case of companies which would not stay in business for long if it were not for the transportation system,

the rates they pay now are bound to go down. However, Mr. Speaker, to be economically viable, these companies will have to consider raising their rates to the levels prevailing for other types of transportation, and unfortunately, the people who will suffer will be the men and women who make far less frequent use of those carriers. If we assume that in future, deregulation will be the norm, competition will be fierce and the big guys more likely to survive than the little guys.
But what is the price we will have to pay? What will be the price of this fierce competition among carriers? We can assume there will be lay-offs. Hundreds of employees will be laid off. There will also be an impact on an equally important area, and I am referring to safety. Transport companies will do whatever they can to deliver, regardless of the safety of goods and passengers. What we cannot accept is that this Government appears to be taking its inspiration from what has been done in the United States, while systematically turning a blind eye to the consequences of that policy in the United States. Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, give an example that says it all. In the United States, deregulation of the air transportation sector took place in 1978. Between 1978 and 1982, full-time employment with U.S. airlines dropped six per cent. Between 1980 and 1985, 40,000 workers lost their jobs in this industry. That is the obvious result of deregulation, which will lead to unbridled competition, where the big guys will have the best chance of winning, at the expense of the little guys. What will happen in the regions? I think that in the short term, we will see small companies closing or going bankrupt, when they are no longer able to face up to the pressures of competition from the big carriers. This will have a disastrous impact on essential jobs in remote areas and on our regional development policies. Not only will there be no improvement, but we will see a deterioration of the situation which will have a further impact on all jobs related to the industry.
Mr. Speaker, there is another situation that also gives cause for concern. Many carriers have had to invest enormous sums of money to obtain the licence that gives them the right to cover a specific territory. Now this legislation will challenge the whole question of the underlying value of these licences, the result being to undermine considerably the assets of these companies which, I think, should have some protection so they can recover costs incurred when servicing remote areas.
Mr. Speaker, there are other considerations as far as jobs are concerned. In addition to the jobs directly related to the transportation industry, there are also jobs in small and medium-sized businesses that depend on that industry. In concluding, I would like to quote from an editorial that appeared in La Presse, which I think quite accurately summarizes the situation. It reads as follows:
We have embarked on an era of deregulation in every field; an era of privatization, in Canada and in Quebec; and an era that celebrates free enterprise and free market competition. Granted, we Canadians who depend on the giant next door are not likely to reverse this trend.
However, we will have to make a choice between what is good for the consumer and what is good for society. Savings to the consumer does not
National Transportation Act, 1986
necessarily mean that society will benefit. Let us first see the price we will have
to pay.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment briefly on the amendment now before the House, an amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). The amendment reads as follows:
"That Bill C-18, an Act respecting national transportation, be not now read a second time but that the Order be discharged, the Bill withdrawn and the subject-matter thereof referred to the Standing Committee on Transport."
Mr. Speaker, I agree that the order should be discharged and the Bill withdrawn now because it is not good for Canada. We do need a study by the Standing Committee on Transport to assess the impact of the proposed deregulation advocated by the Conservative Party of Canada. This Bill is not good for Canada because our country is made up of many regions which are far removed from urban centres and major markets. I am talking about Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver which are Canada's main markets. It would be difficult to implement deregulation. Besides, I am concerned about questions of service and safety.
-of safety. As I said, I have two major concerns about this Bill before us. My number one concern is safety, and my second great concern is service to Canadians.
I come from the riding of Yorkton-Melville. It is a farm riding and there are a number of small villages, towns, communities and farms there. One of my concerns about a law that would deregulate transportation is that the least populated areas, ridings like mine, will not enjoy the same kind of service that Canadians in large central market-places like Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal enjoy. I believe that Saskatchewan, and particularly ridings like mine, will be the losers if transportation in Canada is deregulated. I believe that once again it is an example of the Government across the way following in the footsteps of Ronald Reagan and the American administration.
I am concerned about deregulation from a service point of view because, year after year, I have seen the CNR and the CPR applying to the CTC to abandon rail lines because some towns are small and their elevators may not be very large compared to those in larger centres. The railways have been doing this in an attempt to centralize things. I have also seen the railways campaigning very hard for deregulation and to get rid of the Crow rate so that they may charge a variable rate or a rate the market can bear. Time and time again, I have seen people in small communities having to band together to fight very hard to keep their grain elevators and rail lines and now even to keep their post offices. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you have read recent articles in the press, such as the one this morning in The Globe and Mail, which indicates that 188 rural post offices are to close.

We now have a Minister responsible for Canada Post who is anxious to close down a number of post offices throughout Canada. Mr. Speaker, most of these are in small villages and small towns in Canada. There is a parallel to be drawn between post offices and the transportation system in Canada. As a Member from a rural area I am afraid this Bill will lead to a lack of services, and this is why we must fight tooth and nail to prevent the Minister of Transport from pushing this measure through.
And that is not all, Mr. Speaker. The former Minister and Deputy Prime Minister, the former Member for Yukon, Mr. Erik Nielsen, has been appointed Chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission. I am afraid Mr. Nielsen might not remain neutral in his position because he is the man who led the fight for deregulation in Canada. He is the man who forced the Prime Minister of this Government to introduce the Bill. I am wary of Mr. Nielsen acting as referee in a case like this. I am wary because he believes in the private enterprise system, the private sector, and that spells trouble for people of modest means. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) agrees with me, Mr. Speaker, but I happen to know that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is a redTory.

He is a progressive, red Tory from Manitoba. If he were Minister of Transport, I am sure he would not present a Bill on deregulation under which some of the small centres in his riding would suffer.
I have here in my hands today an application made to the Canadian Transport Commission by Pacific Western Airlines to suspend services on a temporary basis to Whitehorse in the Yukon Territory, effective March 2, 1987, to April 26, 1987. With the abolition of the Canadian Transport Commission under deregulation, we will see more and more of these moves by airline carriers to abandon services to major regional centres.
Coming from Saskatchewan, I know that people complain that Saskatchewan is getting fewer and fewer flights and fewer and fewer choices because the population is not large. If we have wholesale deregulation, there is a concern that seat sales will not be applicable to places like Regina and Saskatoon in the same numbers proportionally as they will be applicable to Vancouver, Montreal and Toronto because there are modes of competition in the larger centres that do not exist on the Prairies. That will be one of the consequences of deregulation. The service in rural Saskatchewan, northern Canada, the Atlantic provinces and throughout much of Quebec will suffer, but that is the kind of vision the Conservative Party has in mind.
When the Canadian people voted for a change in September 1984, they did not vote for a change that would take us on a wild ride in right-wing Conservative politics imported from the United States of America. They were tired of a Liberal Government and a Liberal Prime Minister but they did not
want this Party to go galloping off with Reaganism lock, stock and barrel. Members of our Party will do whatever we can to stop this wholesale deregulation Bill that is before the House
today.
I am also concerned about safety. The experience in the United States has been that airline companies and companies in other modes of transportation are trying to cut services and are trying to cut corners in terms of safety as well. They are doing this because they are trying to save money in the dog-eat-dog world of private enterprise. We should not run the risk of jeopardizing safety in airline services or any other services. My twin concerns are service and safety, but I would like to mention one other thing since I have only two minutes to go.
As a prairie Member, I am concerned as well that as we move down the road to deregulation, we will be moving down the road to variable freight rates across the Prairies. In fact, the CNR now has an application before the CTC to move on variable rates. This is a very important issue for western Canadian farmers. If there are variable freight rates, the railways themselves will determine which communities get services and which communities do not. They can charge rates of 20 per cent or 30 per cent higher for communities where they wish to abandon rail lines. If they charge 20 per cent or 30 per cent more to haul grain to a small community, farmers will haul their grain a few extra miles to a larger community, there will be more and more centralization in larger communities and there will be more and more inland terminals and large through-put elevators, thus leading to the abandonment of rail lines in small communities.
I do not think the railways should make that choice. The CPR and the CNR do not run this country. I think we need regulations that will provide service for ordinary people in Canada, whether they live in Toronto, Ontario, or Kamsack, Saskatchewan.

18 concerning transport deregulation. First I want to say that ever since Confederation the various Governments have used the transport systems and regulated them because they were considered as an essential element of the nation. We need only think about the expanse of this country, the many regions, the myriad of small towns and villages. Without a transport system regulation policy it would be difficult to have a cohesive and united country.
The Liberal Party is aware of the fact that our transport industry is not static by any means and that we cannot allow ourselves to disregard the evolution of transport services elsewhere in the world, more particularly in the United States, our major trade partner. However we condemn any move towards hasty deregulation of the Canadian transport industry which would be pushed through Parliament without due public consultation and adequate study by the Standing Committee on Transport.
Mr. Speaker, I was told that during the two months the Standing Committee on Transport was allotted to study the White Paper Freedom to Move it did not have time to travel to Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Northern Ontario. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, the Standing Committee on Transport could not find time to study the deregulation of the air transport industry which began in the United States in 1978. It is unwise in our view, not to say remiss, to proceed with deregulation in Canada on the basis of a so scanty data base.
Mr. Speaker, despite the objections raised by Liberal Members and indeed a number of Conservative Members, including the committee chairman, because of inadequate time allowed the Transport Committee, Conservative Members supported the report and now we have this Bill. Mr. Speaker, this reminds us of the scenario when the Committee on Government Operations studied Canada Post's corporate plans. The Minister referred them to a committee in order to bring them into full light so that Canadians could understand what those plans were all about, but after one single witness, Canada Post President had appeared for a few days only, Conservative Members in the Committee voted to stop calling in any further witnesses and to submit a report.
Mr. Speaker, that committee was to delve deep into the affairs of the Post Office, and in this case another committee was to lay bare our Canadian transportation system. The conditions were identical, Mr. Speaker-this Government acted in one and the same way, and if we consider the importance of mail delivery in Canada and the importance of transportation, we can conclude that this Government believes in rapid centralization-it wants to make Canada a country of three cities- Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot accept this kind of legislation and the way the Government is ramming it through.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote a few extracts from an article which appeared in the June 27, 1986, issue of the

Mr. Speaker, it was the Minister of State for Small Businesses who was reported as saying that such a Bill was a key element of the economic agenda. In the same article, and I quote again:

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SPACE DEVELOPMENT ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING A TREATY FOR PEACEFUL USE OF SPACE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of drafting and promoting a treaty for the peaceful and non-military uses of space and space based technologies.
She said: Mr. Speaker, when I proposed this motion last fall I was already well aware of Canada's increasing involvement in space activities and shared the growing public concern about the possible uses of space for military rather than peaceful purposes. I have felt strongly for some time that Canada should take a lead in maintaining the frontier of space for peaceful purposes. We have already taken a few steps. For
February 3, 1987

example, there was Canada's participation in the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space; Canada's own admirable space related accomplishments; and our longstanding dedication to international co-operation and the strengthening of the body of international law, for example Canada's long and leading role in the Law of the Sea. These provide a real opening for Canada to take further initiatives in securing the peaceful development of the last frontier.
The time is right for someone, and Canada is an ideal candidate, to propose-indeed, to draft and promote-a treaty for the peaceful and non-military uses of space and space based technologies.
Since last fall we have all become aware of U.S. Defence Department plans to use the NASA International Space Station Project for military and, particularly, SDI purposes. Aviation Week and Space Technology magazine reported the following on December 22:
The U.S. Defence Department has decided to draw formal plans for use of the U.S./intemational space station for military research-Defence Department officials-assert their right to station based research in light of SDI requirements and Defence Space Policy. NASA officials think the Defence Department will use the station for at least basic research related to SDI as well as other military areas.
I repeat the words "at least basic research related to SDI as well as other military areas". This is dreadful news. It is news that raises the real possibility that Canada will become directly involved in the militarization of space, and directly involved in SDI through our participation in the space station. Therefore, there is now a real urgency to address this question. The Government at the moment is being naive, at best, in failing to recognize what is going on both with the space station plans and with the urgent issue of militarization of space.
In responding to this alarming news of United States military/SDI plans for the space station, the director of Canada's space station project buried his head in the sand and said that Canada would continue to participate "until a possible change in policy regarding its use is substantiated". Certainly, a more decisive approach than this is needed.
The United Nations has already decided "as a matter of priority" to seek ways and means of maintaining outer space for peaceful purposes. Its committee established for that purpose is working for, among other things, the banning of weapons in outer space, including anti-satellite weapons; international co-operation in space exploration; the strengthening of international law and institutions for such exploration; the establishment of a World Space Organization; the development of space law and international agreements; greater governmental co-operation; prevention of growing militarization in space; and high level bilateral negotiations between the superpowers, and multilateral negotiations to prevent an arms race in space.
Space Development
Canada should take a lead in drafting and promoting a treaty that would draw on the work of this important com-miteee of the United Nations. Such a treaty would prohibit weapons in space; it would forestall the deployment of antisatellite weapons; it would prevent other types of militarization such as military training, research, and experimentation; it would secure space for exciting, challenging, truly international co-operative ventures designed for the benefit rather than the destruction of humanity.
I would hope that such a treaty would create a world space organization that would concentrate on using space technology for peaceful international activities. Such activities would include communication, navigation, and search and rescue-it should be noted, of course, that Canada, the Soviet Union, France, and the United States are already co-operating in the highly successful SARSAT-remote sensing for agriculture and resource management, meteorology and disaster forecasting, and energy, medical, and biological research. These are some of the activities that a world space organization would undertake.
As well as promoting an urgently needed treaty to prevent the militarization of space, Canada should give careful consideration to a three-stage program, which was discussed at the United Nations last fall, for securing international cooperation and the peaceful uses of space, starting with a special United Nations General Assembly not later than 1990, and leading to co-ordination of national space activities, and ultimately to internationalized direction of the peaceful uses and exploration of space by the year 2000.
Last week, with sadness, we marked the first anniversary of the United States space shuttle tragedy. In December, I had the honour of meeting and having a long discussion with the distinguished Austrian Foreign Minister, Peter Jankowitsch, who for some time was Chairman of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space. I wish to quote from his final statement to that committee before he left New York to resume his position as Foreign Minister of Austria. He said:
The vast benefits that mankind has reaped over past decades from space science and technology, and even more, the tremendous possibilities that still lie ahead, can only lead to one overriding conclusion: the doors to outer space have been thrown wide open and a tremendous job remains to be done. We have created instruments that work, as well as a sense of mission that is quite unique.
We should re-dedicate ourselves, not only to the peaceful conquest of outer space through human beings and through their minds, through ever newer and ever richer technological accomplishments, but also through an increased measure of international co-operation. If we proceed in this spirit, hardly any sacrifice will have been made in vain.
I hope that other Members will join me in calling on Canada to take the lead at the United Nations, and elsewhere, in this mission of knowledge, international co-operation, and peace.
Space belongs to us all. It is not something that a single nation has a right to exploit for its own purposes, particularly military purposes. All nations must work toward the internationalization of space, and we must direct our efforts to the peaceful and non-military uses of space.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SPACE DEVELOPMENT ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING A TREATY FOR PEACEFUL USE OF SPACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the motion presented by the Hon. Member on the other side of the House.
We know that for a number of years, the international community has become increasingly concerned about the possibility of an arms race in outer space. Mr. Speaker, this growing concern reflects an increased awareness on the part of decision-makers and the general public of new technologies of every kind that are making the possibility of using outer space for military as well as for peaceful and beneficial purposes less and less remote.
In fact, since the beginning of the space age, a host of military applications have been developed, mainly for surveillance and communications. The Soviet Union has been one of the leaders in the use of outer space for military purposes. Growing international concern was heightened by President Reagan's announcement in 1983 about a major research program that would examine the feasibility of an ABM defence system, including weapons based in space.
President Reagan's announcement was not the cause of the concern about the military use of outer space although it did much to increase it.
The main multilateral forums before which this issue is dealt with in the context of disarmament and arms control are the First Committee of the UN General Assembly and the Geneva Conference on Disarmament. In 1981, the UN General Assembly started discussing ways to prevent an arms race in outer space. Ever since, this matter has been on the agenda of the First Committee of the UN General Assembly.
During its 1985 session, the Conference on Disarmament agreed for the first time on the terms of reference of a special committee charged with discussing prevention of an arms race in outer space. Mr. Speaker, those terms of reference, which did not include negotiations, were renewed and only slightly modified at the 1986 session.
Canada played an active role in the discussion and debate on this issue at the First Committee and the Conference on Disarmament. At the First Committee of the UN General Assembly, non-aligned countries have traditionally been the most progressive.
At the 1985 and 1986 sessions of the First Committee, the Canadian delegation worked closely with the Western delegations and members of the group of non-aligned countries to achieve a consensus on an appropriate resolution. These efforts have been largely successful so far, and Canada was able to join the other delegations in supporting a resolution that was adopted without dissent.
Whereas the debates of the first commission reflect, at the political level, the significance of various concerns and the national interest, the disarmament commission was the forum for more serious discussions on different legal, technical and
political aspects of the use of outer space. Canada's contribution to these debates ranks among the best.
At the 1985 session we presented a working paper which was an in-depth study of current international legislation concerning arms control and outer space. During last year's session we produced a document dealing more specifically with the use of terminology.
Undeniably, our contributions gave a sense of direction to the commission debates and made it a lot easier to make the participants more aware of the complex process involved in drafting international legislation governing military and nonmilitary use of outer space. Canada is hopeful that during the 1987 session which will open soon it will be possible to reach early agreement on a mandate which will pave the way for further studies in this field.
The activities of Canada within these two multilateral key forums attests to the Government's firm commitment to promote the peaceful use of, and the prevention of the arms race in, outer space. The efforts made to this end within these forums should, we believe, support and complement the bilateral discussions held by the United States and the U.S.S.R. in the course of their Geneva negotiations on nuclear and space issues which, as you know, have the same objective. Mr. Speaker, we are confident that Canadians endorse our approach.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SPACE DEVELOPMENT ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING A TREATY FOR PEACEFUL USE OF SPACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the spirit of the resolution put forward by the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) and to take serious objection to the gobbledegook we have just heard.

-of the Government spokesman who has uttered a number of meaningless words.

The fact of the matter is that it is embarrassing and deplorable that a Government could respond to such a resolution with fluffery and without addressing the central issue about which people around the world are deeply concerned, that is, the ongoing development of the Strategic Defence Initiative and the clear determination on the part of the Reagan administration to deploy that system in space at the earliest possible opportunity.
For the Parliamentary Secretary to stand in the House for 10 minutes and not deal with that central issue and pretend somehow that it was an intelligent and rational response could only bring the most anguished cry of shame that the Government ignores a compelling imperative which the country must address-the fundamental problem of how we control that clear determination of our close ally.
February 3, 1987

I believe this Private Member's Motion represents the concern felt by many Canadians. I see that the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary thinks it is a joke. There are millions of Canadians who do not think the SDI is a joke, but they may think that the Government is a joke. Certainly the polls show that most Canadians think the Government is a joke. The fact of the matter is that this issue is nothing to laugh about. It goes to the very heart of what we as a country are prepared to do to provide a different response to the arms race.
The Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam was quite right in saying that we are at a very important turning point and that all the work done in committees of the United Nations and by others stands as a very feeble defence against the determination of the Reagan administration to proceed.
It was frightening to read the speech of Secretary of Defence Caspar Weinberger as reported in The New York Sunday Times indicating that the intent of that administration was to move toward deployment of the SDI before its term of office is over and to so develop this crazy and wild scheme that successive administrations will not be able to turn it back. I only regret that the chief spokesman for our Government did not try to come to grips with that issue in some sensitive way rather than present the silliness we heard.
For the moment I want to address my remarks to the Hon. Member who presented the resolution before us. I think there is a flaw in the resolution, which does not in any way distract from its spirit or purpose. The resolution itself talks about the militarization of space. We must be careful and clear in recognizing that it is important to maintain certain of the present military aspects of space as a form of detection, surveillance, and verification. If the resolution had talked about the elimination of weapons in space, I think it would have been much clearer.
When the Hon. Member refers to the military use or application of space, I do not believe she is promoting the abolition of various forms of satellites presently used to gain information and which could be and must be used as a way of maintaining stability. In this terrible, maniacal world with the nuclear genie out of the bottle, one of the forces of stability is the capacity of both major nuclear powers to have a fairly clear sense of information about what the other side is up to.
I pose a question which I believe I heard in the Hon. Member's remarks: how do we go from an exchange of the satellite technology which is now used for surveillance and verification into a kind of controlled management outside the capacity of the military, into an internationalization of it, or into space agencies of a domestic kind which must maintain that form of gathering information and therefore must maintain the technology?
For example, in the case of Canada it may be a realistic proposition that we as a country want to develop our own satellite technology as a way of protecting our own sovereignty and of providing an independent form of detection of the various machinations of the superpowers in our own space.
Space Development
Satellite technology may be used as an adjunct to do that. We would not want to give that away, just as I think it would be important for us to contribute. I fully endorse the spirit of the Hon. Member's resolution toward the internationalization of that kind of control. However, it is in a sense a military use of space. The proper definition would be that we do not want to weaponize space or use it for its offensive capability or capacity.
I draw that to the Hon. Member's attention because she was not at a meeting which we had a week or so ago with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). At that time we said it would be very important for the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade to examine carefully the arms control questions relating to space.
For example, it would be very important for us to decide what is the definition of "research" as defined by the Americans when it comes to the ABM Treaty and its use of SDI. We need that kind of expert advice. I think we as a Parliament should proceed with a very careful study of the arms control aspects of space technology as it applies to our own purposes, as it applies to the developments of the superpowers, and as it applies to the potential that we would have to employ this technology in the United Nations or through an international space agency.
It is a case where one must marry the technology to politics. One must marry the philosophy or the morality of the use of space to the increasing and highly complex technology which is being employed. Certainly the thrust of the Hon. Member's remarks that this is not something which must be confined in a secret or covert way inside the Pentagon or the Kremlin is something that other countries can abide or tolerate.
We must have a much broader and open control of management of space technology and use it to provide both stability in the arms race and, hopefully, its eventual elimination. That may mean that we will have to use technology in space and we should not be attempting to eliminate or abolish it. I suppose in a perfect world it could be, but unfortunately once we develop a technology, someone will try to use it. The best way to offset that is to ensure that we have adequate capability of detection, surveillance, or observation of what other countries are doing.
I agree fully with the Hon. Member that the way we do it now is wrong and leads to instability. Where it is particularly wrong is in terms of the initiatives to turn the technology of space into an aggressive offensive weapons system. That is something to which the Government must say no, but it refuses to do so. It must say no to the efforts of the United States to broaden the interpretation of the ABM Treaty, to wit, as we heard President Reagan, after the Reykjavik meeting, say that the United States intended to test and develop space weapons. That was clearly a break with the proper rules and laws of the ABM Treaty.

February 3, 1987

Why does our Government refuse to speak out on this issue, why does it tend to say that the Americans really are not talking about a broad interpretation? It comes to me as a great regret that we seem to be avoiding coming to grips with the issue, something about which there would be total agreement in Canada. I do not know of any Canadian who wants further weaponization of space. What is the Government hiding from? Why is the Government not prepared to take a firmer, clearer stand on this crucial issue? What is it that we have to lose? Are we afraid that somehow we will once again run counter to the wishes of the Reagan administration? Is that what is holding us up?
Surely, Mr. Speaker, in an issue as crucial and as universal in its application, this is an area where the Mulroney Government can afford to say no for once. It is important that it do that, because as we saw in Reykjavik on this one issue alone, on the ability to come to some decision to halt the development of an SDI program rests the opportunity to move toward the abolition, elimination or reduction of offensive nuclear weapons, if we could get our American allies to agree with us. I think it is important that a country like Canada speak out to provide that persuasion. We can make then a breakthrough for which the world has been yearning for four years. I think we should support the spirit of the resolution, even though I think the wording of it is something that leaves some questions in mind.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   SPACE DEVELOPMENT ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING A TREATY FOR PEACEFUL USE OF SPACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome heartily the introduction of this motion, partly because it focuses the attention of the House on an area of Government that for years has received scant attention, namely, the whole area of External Affairs and the relationship between this country and the rest of the world, and more particularly because it focuses our attention on space. This is surely the avenue for the human race to follow in the future, especially as we approach the 21st century when, as possibly never before, the human race will see an opportunity for the expansion of our life.
I am delighted that the House has a chance to debate the subject of outer space, I hope not, as in the course of the rest of the day, as Government and Opposition, but recalling that this is Private Members' Hour. We are not here speaking as members of the Opposition or members for the Government but, rather, as Members of Parliament sharing concerns that we have as Canadian representatives.
I support the principle of the motion, but I, like the previous speaker, have reservations about the wording. One could infer that there was no such treaty, that there was nothing now in existence and having an effect upon the way in which nations conduct themselves vis-a-vis outer space. The fact is that we have 17 treaties and covenants to which this country has been a party. Canada has given leadership since 1959 when the
Committee for Peaceful Uses of Outer Space was first formed by the United Nations and to which since then for almost a generation Canada has been a party. During those years the various countries participating have produced such treaties and covenants as these: the Outer Space Treaty, the Moon Treaty, the ABM Treaty, the two SALT Treaties, the Threshold Ban Treaties, the Peaceful Nuclear Explosions Treaty, the Partial Test Ban Treaty and the Environmental Modification Treaty. We have had an extraordinary, impressive list of international agreements by which the nations of the world have come to grips with this unprecedented challenge, which indicate how Canada and the various Governments are endeavouring, in a responsible, co-operative, way to face the challenge that the development of outer space presents.
I would like to see some attention in this debate focus upon the positive way in which the peaceful uses of outer space can be developed. Let me tell the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) to keep listening. I fully concur with the concern about the demilitarization of space and about the deweaponization of space, but I would like the record of this debate to show some fuller attention given to the technological, scientific, productive development of space, because peace is not simply a matter of excluding conflict, but also a matter of developing the opportunities for the human race to lead a fuller life.
I believe that is what we are doing now and what Canada has in the past two years, endeavoured to do through its international negotiations and activities. We have, for example, entered into a partnership with the United States manned space station project which can be a very productive, salutary, positive development for the U.S. and Canada. We have reached out to Europe in a co-operative venture, being a partner in several programs initiated by the European Space Agency. We have invited other countries to co-operate with us, particularly in the RadarSat remote sensing project which is the chief Canadian effort, the one in which Canadian expertise and leadership can have the most positive, lasting contribution to the world.
Important as the prod, the stimulus and the inspiration of this motion can be to the House today, I believe it is vital that we recognize what Canada has been doing and build on that foundation. I believe that the advent of the Canadian Space Agency announced in the Speech from the Throne that began this session offers us the promise and the expectation of that. That agency can co-ordinate the existing programs. It can initiate new endeavours and thereby offer us an opportunity to develop and progress, which is much needed.
In the remaining time available to me, Mr. Speaker, I want to focus attention on the other dimension of this motion, which is concern about the peaceful use of outer space with particular application to demilitarization and deweaponization, the avoidance of conflict and the avoidance of the use of outer space as a way by which new military power can be asserted by one nation or a group of nations over others. It is vital that we recognize that already in the absence of clear, comprehensive
February 3, 1987

treaties, such as this motion would call for, there is nonetheless some basis in international law that seeks to achieve the objectives which I would believe would be the purpose of the treaty to which the motion refers. For instance, certain military activities in outer space can now be held to be inconsistent with international law, such as interference with space based remote sensors that could be used for military purposes as between the U.S.A. and the U.S.S.R.; the placement of nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around the earth and on celestial bodies or in orbit around them; hostile acts through the use of force on celestial bodies and the orbits around them; the placement of military bases and conduct of military tests or manoeuvres on celestial bodies and in orbits around them; the testing of nuclear weapons in outer space; the development, testing, and deployment of space based ABM systems or components; and the military or hostile use of environmental modification techniques in outer space.
It is true that this corpus of international law does not meet all the needs. It certainly does not exclude the challenge which the motion and its proponent addressed namely, the hazard that has been brought before us anew by the possibility of a strategic defence program. We will not be unmindful in debating this, but Canada has decisively refused as a country and a Government to be a party to the research dimension of that Strategic Defence Initiative.
Let us recognize that. We have not refused to recognize the potential validity of SDI in the hands of the United States but we as a country have not participated actively in it. Let us therefore recognize that as we contemplate the possibility of a Strategic Defence Initiative by the United States or its equivalent by the Soviet Union, something which we should not refuse to recognize as being a serious possibility, the world at large faces a previously unknown hazard, and this must concern the House as it must concern the nation. Therefore, I would welcome the prospect envisioned by this motion of focusing anew on the need for further and fuller agreements between nations with respect to the use of outer space for military purposes.
I do not assume that one treaty can be like one magic wand that will remove the danger. Rather, I would think in terms of future agreements building on the foundation I have outlined in these remarks. Whether we are talking about one more treaty, a series of them or amendments to existing agreements, I would hope that we would be committed to the removal of the hazard of destruction to the world that is now before us through the technological use of outer space. I would hope that we would recognize that we have a new frontier and a new opportunity and that we as a human race should be prepared to use it for the future life of man rather than for future destruction.

They slashed the budget of the National Research Council and, after having promised to restore the previous Government's cuts, they slashed the budget for post-secondary education. speechtext:
In fact, Mr. Speaker, I have consulted with the mover of the motion on this point. The point I am trying to make, if the majority Party will not, in an undemocratic fashion, take away my right to speak, is that those budget cuts were made to established programs used for peaceful purposes in order to find $800 million for the space station. What is the purpose of the space station? We were told at the time that its purpose was peaceful research. There was an understanding that it would not be used for military purposes. Now the cat is out of the bag, and that undemocratic decision to give $800 million to the space station has been exposed by the American decision to use the space station for purposes of war. In other words, the Americans practised a little deceit for a year, and this Government accepted at face value their vague statement that it was to be used for peaceful purposes. Therefore, because these things have been done in an undemocratic way, the effect is that research for war and SDI in that space station has taken $800 million away from peaceful programs in Canada. That action is highly undemocratic.
If the Government had bluntly told the Canadian people that it wished to give $800 million to star wars by contributing it to the space station, the Canadian people would have objected even more strongly than they did when the joint committee heard people all across Canada tell the Government to stay out of star wars. If the people had been told that star wars would take away money from the NRC, universities and research in the humanities and science, they would have reacted much more strongly.
My point is that we need legislation such as the legislation for which the mover of the motion, the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett), has asked. We need legislation democratically based and passed by this Parliament so that the Government is obliged to follow the principles of it. The Government would not then, I would hope, imagine that it had the freedom to take such an autocratic action as it has taken in the funding of the space station.
As has been pointed out by all three previous speakers, there are many important peaceful uses for research into peaceful activities in space. We need those peaceful activities and the entire world needs them. Yes, I agree with the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry to the extent that one of those activities should be surveillance since there are still warlike activities to be surveyed. However, that should be done through the United Nations. If the space station is to be used for surveillance, it should be directed and controlled by the United Nations, the only international authority that has any standing between the two superpowers that may be engaged in space warfare or war-related space research. Again that should
be legislated in this Parliament. That is to say, it should be legislated that our contribution to any space station should be based only on a clear agreement that it would be under the direction of the UN. Therefore, any surveillance of military activities, on the ground or in space, would be carried out for the benefit of all the people of the world. It would not be just for the benefit of the U.S. military, who will of course keep secret any results of military surveillance, military testing, or military uses of the space station they expect us to help pay for. Under the UN a space station would be capable of pursuing to the benefit of all peoples in the world both the broad range of peaceful uses which the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) has read out and the other two speakers have agreed to, but also any necessary surveillance of potential warlike activities. However, that will not happen unless in Canada and other countries democratic legislation such as this motion proposes is adopted in order to control the Governments and their representatives, military representatives above all, who engage in other kinds of adventures in space.
I hope the House will accept in due course the position put forward by the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam and bring this matter to fruition through discussion and a vote in this Parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to speak to the motion presented by the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett). This is indeed a serious matter, and I am surprised that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy)-unfortunately he is not in the House to hear what I have to say, and I hope he will be able to read this in Hansard tomorrow-should come here to tell us that the Canadian Government has not taken seriously the issue of the peaceful use of space. I would call that not bad faith but at least gross negligence. Often the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry has given us such a variety of opinions on Canada's role in space agencies or on Canadian defence policy that there is something for everyone. It is difficult to know exactly where he stands or in fact where his party stands on issues of this magnitude. In fact, this lack of focus should not be surprising. We have seen how this kind of attitude put a crushing financial burden on this country, which in thse difficult times makes decisions often far more difficult. Because we have to live with a problematic financial situation, it becomes increasingly difficult to make decisions that require a financial commitment from the Government. I think it was with this in mind that in the past the Government reacted as it did to the issue of the peaceful use of space.
Suggesting, as the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam did just now, that Canadian diplomacy be engaged in vast U.N. manoeuvres-with all due respect-practically
February 3, 1987

ignores the progress accomplished by the community of nations in developing a law of space and especially the problems raised by the use of outer space for peaceful purposes.
Mr. Speaker, I think this underestimates the role of the committee on the peaceful use of outer space and the relevance of the issues it is considering at this time.
Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of our colleagues who sit on the Opposition benches on the other side of the House, allow me to recall briefly how the United Nations have evolved over the nearly 30 years since they first got involved in the great space exploration adventure, the most recent and undoubtedly the most challenging human epic.
Back in 1958, after man put the first artificial satellite Sputnik into earth orbit, the General Assembly of the United Nations established an ad hoc committee of 18 nations which a year later, pursuant to Resolution 1472, became the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space.
So today we are being urged to launch a new study or finalization process which should eventually lead to a treaty on this issue. This may sound just fine at first, but why ignore and forget what has been done in the past and what is still being done today? As I see it, Canada has always been directly involved, and later on in my remarks I will quote a supportive statement to that effect. Members of this House-indeed the Member of our Party who had the floor a few minutes ago raised this issue before the United Nations last year.
Since 1961 the standing committee-now made up of 53 member countries-has represented the interests of humanity and now includes countries which have the technical know-how required to send satellites into orbit or can produce the systems and subsystems carried aloft by modern communications or earth observation satellites. I might also mention the ever larger group of nations anxious to share in the economic, scientific and humanitarian benefits which the peaceful use of outer space has put within our reach.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to make a brief review of these questions which are being dealt with by and are of particular interest to the committee. First, the review of the impact of international cooperation in the peaceful use of outer space; the establishment of international co-operation programs which might be carried out under the auspices of the United Nations; the promotion of applied research and the peaceful use of space; the distribution of research information; and the study of legal problems created by space exploration.
That committee is already committed and the Hon. Member would like us to recommit ourselves into another process-but we know how much time and energy are needed to take part in international agencies and how difficult and costly it can be, but just the same we should not hesitate to do so. It is very difficult to reach a consensus, as everyone knows. Imagine what waste of time it would be if we launched into a new crusade to reach the same goals. Of course, we should not
National Transportation Act, 1986
neglect, nor forget the Hon. Member's good faith in this process, in the idea she had for putting the motion forward, but I feel that at this time we already have another agency, a committee and we should follow on the course already taken.
The work of the committee in the area of space law is extensive, and it is because of this that we have negotiated and submitted to the U.N. Assembly the following treaties. The treaty dealing with the principles governing actvities of states on atmospheric space exploration and utilization, including the earth and other celestial bodies-I am quoting rapidly, Mr. Speaker, I know my time is going fast, I am already in the atmosphere at least-agreements on astronauts' rescue; the return of astronauts and the return of objects launched into space; the convention on international responsibility for damage caused by space objects; the convention on the registration of objects launched into extra atmospheric space; the agreement on activities of states on the moon and on other celestial bodies. A whole series of treaties on which we worked as a member country of the United Nations, and on which we will keep on working.
It is my view, Mr. Speaker, that Canada has amply done its part, and that this Government's commitment to international agencies and to the Canadian people are in line with what Canadians want.
